processing: Grown under shade and made mainly into gyokuro; breeding trials also found it performs well as tencha for matcha.
harvest_season: Early to mid spring, about two days before Yabukita.
appearance_dry: As gyokuro, a green leaf with good colour and sheen.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Kyoto gyokuro: a clear pale green-yellow.
appearance_wet: Medium-sized green shoots, tender as with other shaded teas.
taste_profile: Rated highly for gyokuro quality; expect the rich umami and sweetness usual for shaded Uji tea rather than a known signature flavour.

brewing.notes: Usual gyokuro settings. Patience and cool water matter more than the exact timing.

vintage_note: Rarely sold under its own name; it usually goes into Kyoto gyokuro and matcha. As with other shaded Japanese teas, it is sold from the current spring's harvest. A single-cultivar lot should state the grower and year.
description:
Ujimidori is a Kyoto cultivar selected from native Uji plants for gyokuro. Kyoto's tea researchers list it among the main gyokuro plants of the prefecture, alongside Gokou, Kyomidori, Ujihikari and Samidori.

Its appeal to growers is practical: it buds about two days ahead of Yabukita, grows vigorously early on, and gives a yield at least as good. Its gyokuro earns high marks for colour, sheen and inner quality.

Little has been written about its taste on its own. Treat it as you would any good gyokuro: a small pot, cool water, a long first steep, and short steeps after that.

It turned up well in Kyoto's trials for tencha too, so you may be drinking it in matcha without knowing. Named lots are uncommon, and worth trying when you find them.
history: Ujimidori was selected from native Uji varieties under the line name Kyoken 307 and completed in 1983, per the Kyoto Prefectural Tea Research Institute. Little else about its spread is documented.
